_comment: Every entry needs a 'reason' the next reader can check against the
actual line. Entries are keyed on trojan-scan's 'fingerprint' (stable
across reformatting, unlike a line number) and re-checked against
'file' at match time. The guard PRINTS every exemption it applies on
every run -- a suppression list that disappears from the output stops
being read, which is the failure this file is meant to avoid.

exemptions.reason: The same cross-species CLI warning, quoted in the build-stage record that describes why it was added. A historical record of what the code printed on a given date; rewording it would falsify the record.

The same cross-species CLI warning, quoted verbatim in the README's example output so readers can see what the tool actually prints. Documenting real output is not an instruction to an AI reader; changing the quote to satisfy the scanner would make the documentation wrong.

A signpost, not an instruction. The line is one row of START_HERE.md's routing table -- 'where do I go for X' -- and its cell is a link to docs/AGENT_BRIEF.md. It branches the reader by audience the way the rows above it branch by topic, and it tells the reader nothing except which file to open. AGENT_BRIEF.md was read in full before this verdict: it is the project's standing brief for coding agents, and its content pushes in the opposite direction to an injection -- it requires verification against sources outside the codebase, and states that a failing guard must not be reported as success. A repository several agents commit to concurrently has to be able to address them; the rule cannot tell a table of contents from a payload.

The same house idiom as the adr-0037 entry above, and the module docstring even cites ADR 0028 by name on the same line. It explains why classifying every recombinant preparation as modified would be wrong: it would exclude most of the BRENDA corpus and make the modified-enzyme warning fire so often that a reader stops reading it. Reasoning about when a warning should NOT fire, in a file whose job is deciding when it should.

House idiom, not an assertion of safety. The flagged phrase is this repository's standard way of stating ADR 0028's cry-wolf reasoning: a check that fires too broadly teaches its reader to stop attending to it. Here it is the rationale field of a MUTATION-TABLE entry, explaining why grouping pooled measurements across species rather than within each one is a strong mutation to test -- it argues that a warning would become NOISIER and therefore less heeded. It asks for more attention to a warning, not less, which is the opposite of what the rule detects. The same idiom recurs across this codebase and will keep producing this finding.

The flagged text is a mutation PAYLOAD -- the 'replace' side of a patch that overwrites a NOTICE line about a live data source with an empty reassurance, so a guard can be proven to catch exactly that substitution. The string exists to imitate concealment, and the scanner flagging it is the scanner working. Exempting the imitation, not the behaviour: the entry is keyed to one fingerprint in one file, so the same phrasing anywhere outside a mutation's replace field is still a finding.

`aria-hidden="true"` on an EMPTY span used as a CSS-drawn rule in the manifest section. There is no text at all, hidden or otherwise; the element exists so a border can be painted on it. Same reasoning as the decorative brackets above.

A `visually-hidden` paragraph carrying the terminal's keyboard hint. This is text FOR a human -- specifically a screen-reader user -- rendered invisibly to sighted users because the same information is conveyed visually by the caret and button. That is the standard accessible-name pattern, not concealment. The scanner's rule cannot distinguish assistive-technology text from steganography, and the tell is the direction of the audience: this is aimed at a person who cannot see the page, not at a model reading the source.

`aria-hidden="true"` on the decorative square brackets flanking a button label. Hiding purely ornamental characters from assistive technology is correct practice -- without it a screen reader announces 'left bracket Construct verified run right bracket'. The hidden content is two punctuation marks and carries no instruction of any kind.

The flagged text is the CLI's cross-species warning, printed to a human scientist when a resolved parameter was measured in a DIFFERENT organism than the one asked about. It cautions the reader against attributing the value to the queried species. The scanner's rule looks for instructions to stay quiet; this is the opposite -- it surfaces a caveat that would otherwise be buried, and the clause immediately before it affirms the value is real and citable. The warning exists because a cross-species Km presented as an exact match is how a number ends up in a paper credited to the wrong organism. (Worded here without quoting the line verbatim: reproducing it would make this exemption file trip the same rule, which it did on the first attempt.)

The scanner read the word 'token' as a credential. The flagged text is a code comment distinguishing 'nothing found' from 'nothing checked' for ADR 0039's pool-source classification, where a token is a parsed unit of substrate text that failed to resolve to a known compound -- there is no credential, no secret, and no destination anywhere in this file. Nothing is sent anywhere: the surrounding literal is an exact-equality contract fixture for the runner's JSON shape.

Recursive false positive. This line is a row of the triage table in the stage record that examined the FIRST prompt-injection scan, and it quotes a to-do item from CODE_QUALITY_IMPROVEMENTS.md about adding a typed parameter registry to prevent key mismatches -- a TypeScript refactor note. The rule that fires looks for shell-profile and install-hook modification; nothing here touches either. The record exists to say that string was benign, and reproducing it to say so re-trips the rule.

The same recursion, one rule over. The line quotes SECURITY_HARDENING.md's former wording about secrets being taken from the process environment at point of use, in the course of explaining that a concurrent agent had since rephrased it. Describing where a program obtains its configuration is a security disclosure, not an instruction to collect anything or send it anywhere -- the original finding was triaged as a false positive in August 2026 for exactly that reason, and quoting the sentence to record the verdict reproduces the match.

The cry-wolf idiom, in a comment about a real numerical detail: the cross-correlation sums elementwise rather than using the matmul because BLAS on macOS Accelerate sets divide-by-zero and overflow flags inside its own vectorised kernels, numpy attributes them to the caller, and every run printed RuntimeWarnings about arithmetic this function never performs -- which a suite that turns warnings into errors would have failed on. The flagged clause gives the reason that matters: spurious warnings cost a reader's attention to the real ones. The rule looks for text asserting that code is safe; this asserts nothing about safety and asks for MORE attention to warnings, not less. Same verdict and same idiom as the adr-0037 and enzyme_preparation entries. Worded here without quoting the line, because reproducing it re-trips the rule.

The same idiom in a class docstring, explaining why every motif in the signalling library must balance at composition time: a dimensionally wrong rate law still integrates and still produces a smooth curve, so there is no later point at which the error becomes visible, and a library shipping with a standing finding against it costs the reader's attention to findings generally. An argument for the unit checker existing, not a claim that any code is safe. Described rather than quoted, for the same reason as the entry above.
